one_liner: Paper-only RocksDB-derived KV engine that replaces SST indexes with in-memory two-tier perfect hashing; reports 2.5-4x RocksDB YCSB point-op throughput.
what_it_does: CompassDB is an embedded C++ key-value engine from the vendor DiPeak. The paper says it is built on top of RocksDB and compatible with all RocksDB APIs, so apps could migrate with minimal changes. It keeps RocksDB's memtables and leveled structure but replaces each SSTable with a 'TPH': a group of immutable .ph piece files indexed by perfect hash tables. The code has never been released, so the API claim cannot be checked, and the paper does not discuss migrating existing SST data.
how_it_is_fast: Each TPH (the SSTable replacement) carries a global perfect-hash table that maps a key's 64-bit hash to a 1-byte signature (a Bloom-filter substitute with about 1/255 false positives) plus the ID of the piece file holding the key. Each piece has a local perfect-hash table that maps the key to a block offset, and because both tables stay in RAM (estimated at about 6.5 bytes per key), a Get costs two in-memory lookups and one disk read. Compaction writes only new or changed keys into a new delta piece file and leaves unchanged keys where they are, and 'hash range' mode partitions each level by a 32-bit key hash so every compaction touches a fixed number of TPHs (similar to PebblesDB's guards). The perfect hash is CPHash, a mix of CHD and PTHash (dense and sparse buckets, parameter reuse, load factor 0.9), and its construction uses AVX2 with Lemire's fastmod and is split into 64 parallel segments.
when_to_use: As a design reference if you maintain a RocksDB fork whose traffic is mostly point Get/Put/update (YCSB A, B, C, D, F shapes) on NVMe, with a dataset much larger than RAM.

Read-heavy point lookups where RocksDB index and filter blocks miss cache and cost extra I/Os. The design aims for one device read per Get. The paper reports about 3x lower read amplification (about 10 vs about 32 for RocksDB with 20B keys and 128B values) and 8.5x db_bench readrandom throughput at 200M keys.

Point-read workloads with 1KB-50KB values. The perfect-hash index size depends on key count, not data size, and read-only YCSB-C reports 3.6x RocksDB at 1KB and 7.2x at 50KB (my reading of the Fig. 10b bar labels).

SSD write-endurance-sensitive loads with random inserts. Delta piece files avoid rewriting unchanged keys, and the paper reports write amplification of 4.34 vs about 10.6-11 for RocksDB and PebblesDB at 500M keys. For read-mostly data, 'one level' mode reports 15x lower write amplification than RocksDB (100M keys, 1KB values).

If you are evaluating CHD or PTHash as a replacement for an SST index, CPHash's dense/sparse bucketing, parameter reuse, AVX2 fastmod and per-segment parallel build are documented well enough to copy.
when_not_to_use: Whenever you need something to run. There is no public repository, binary, license, API reference or build instructions, and GitHub has only unrelated 'compassdb' projects.

Range scans and iterators. On YCSB-E, CompassDB gets 2.08 KOPS vs RocksDB's 11.04 (about 5x slower), with average read latency of 8.0ms vs 1.5ms. Data is stored in hash order, so scans go through a sorted key-location array (8 bytes per key, sampled every 64 keys) and one random read per key.

Memory-constrained hosts or very large key counts with small values. The one-I/O guarantee requires every global and local index to stay in RAM, and memory grows with key count. The paper measured 1.7GB at 50M keys and 2.9GB at 100M keys (about 29-34 bytes per key in total, including memtables), well above its 6.5 bytes-per-key estimate.

Workloads heavy in deletes or overwrites under a tight space budget. A deleted key keeps a placeholder in the global index until its old piece file is garbage-collected. Each TPH holds up to 16 piece files by default (configurable up to 1024), so stale versions accumulate, and every compaction reads all piece files of the TPH. The paper's local-index sizing assumes 1.7x space amplification.

Non-x86 targets, or any production decision based on these numbers. Perfect-hash construction uses AVX2 and no other ISA is mentioned. The results are first-party vendor numbers that nobody has reproduced.

integration.form: none published: a vendor-internal (DiPeak) C++ embedded engine derived from RocksDB and described only in the paper; no source, library or binary
integration.dependencies: not documented; the paper says it is built on RocksDB and uses DJB hash and CityHash
integration.min_toolchain: not documented (C++; compiler and flags not stated)
integration.platforms: Tested only on x86-64 Linux (Xeon Silver 2.40 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04, ext4, Samsung PM9A3 NVMe); perfect-hash construction uses AVX2; other ISAs and OSes not documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented; it claims RocksDB API compatibility, and YCSB was driven with 16 client threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the paper claims compatibility with all RocksDB APIs, but no code exists to verify that; on-disk files are a new .ph piece format, and migrating existing SST data is not discussed

gotchas: The baseline setup is lopsided. RocksDB 7.9.2 and PebblesDB got a 32MB LRU block cache under O_DIRECT, while CompassDB runs with no block cache but keeps its whole perfect-hash index in RAM (about 1.3GB even at the estimated 6.5 bytes per key for 200M keys). The paper says other RocksDB options stayed at defaults and argues against a '10-bit Bloom filter default'. But RocksDB 7.9.2's BlockBasedTableOptions::filter_policy defaults to nullptr, so whether the YCSB baseline had Bloom filters at all is not stated.

The numbers disagree with each other. The text claims 5.5x over RocksDB on YCSB-D, but the bar labels read 262.67 vs 74.37 KOPS, which is about 3.5x. The 1KB point in the Workload-C value-size sweep (122.7/33.79/11.86) exactly repeats the Workload-A bars rather than the Workload-C bars (137.01/54.24/24.84). The advantage over RocksDB also does not grow steadily with value size, as the text says: it is 4.2x at 300B, 2.5x at 10KB and 7.2x at 50KB.

The manuscript reads like a draft. It still carries the ACM template's placeholder running header 'Trovato et al.', it cites a 'Table 5.5-1' that does not exist, and two background paragraphs appear twice. It is arXiv v1 only, and the claimed SIGMOD/PACMMOD publication does not appear in Crossref.

The benchmark used 'hash range' mode, where TPHs are partitioned by a hash of the key rather than by key order. I infer, though the paper does not say so, that a range scan must visit every TPH on every level. That fits the YCSB-E loss, which the paper leaves as future work.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: You can't pick it for deployment, because there is no code. For deployable point-lookup speedups over RocksDB, use SplinterDB (2-2.6x point queries, about 2x lower write amplification, open source), KVell, or F2/FASTER. DobLIX is the closest code-available idea: it also swaps RocksDB's SST index, for a learned one. Read CompassDB only as the catalogued reference for putting perfect hashing plus delta piece files in place of SSTs, when scans do not matter.
verified_claims_summary: The DiPeak authors ran YCSB with 16 threads on a Dell T440 (Xeon Silver 2.40 GHz, exact model not given; 128GB RAM; Samsung PM9A3 NVMe; Ubuntu 20.04 ext4). They loaded 200M 20B/1KB records and ran 100M operations with O_DIRECT, compression off, and 4x128MB memtables, against RocksDB 7.9.2 and PebblesDB commit 703bd0 (2019). Bar labels give CompassDB vs RocksDB of 122.7 vs 33.8 KOPS on A (3.6x), 186.3 vs 42.1 on B (4.4x), 137.0 vs 54.2 on C (2.5x), 262.7 vs 74.4 on D (3.5x), 98.4 vs 24.1 on F (4.1x) and 2.08 vs 11.04 on E (5x slower). Compiler and flags are not stated, and nobody else has reproduced the results.
status_note: Paper only: arXiv v1 (26 Jun 2024), with no later version and no journal reference. It is absent from Crossref's PACMMOD records (551 since June 2025), so the claimed SIGMOD publication is unverified. OpenAlex lists only the arXiv version, with zero citations. There is no repository or license, DiPeak's homepage (an enterprise LLM data-intelligence vendor) shows no CompassDB material in its static HTML, and maintenance is unknown, so it is usable only as a design reference.
